occupation.note: 'Daniel Elston & [illegible]', soap and candle manufactory, paying cash for tallow and house ashes - Chicago Democrat, 26 November 1833. The word after the ampersand is obliterated by an ink blot on the scan and 'Co.' is a reasonable expansion rather than a reading.

persons.note: A MANUFACTURER, WHICH THE 1835 TOWN HAS ALMOST NONE OF. Buying tallow and house ashes is buying the by-products of the packing trade and of every household fire in the town, which makes this one business a measure of how many households there were. Andreas has a Daniel Elston running the largest of the city's five brickyards by 1854 - two decades past the scene and evidence of nothing about 1835 except that the man stayed. The Chicago Democrat of 26 November 1833 is the only contemporary Chicago document this project holds; an advertiser in it was paying to be found, which makes it strong evidence of existence and address in November 1833 and weak evidence of survival to 1 July 1835, nineteen months and about 2,400 people later. FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 2 times in its two later lists: the poll of Chicago's first city election, 2 May 1837 — “Daniel Elston” (f1839_v0500, printed page 44, ward 4, voting for John H. Kinzie); the city register of 1839 — “Daniel Elston” as school inspector (f1839_r0039, printed page 38). What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago on 2 May 1837 and in that ward. It is written as 1837 evidence with describes_date 1837-05-02, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. The ward is a location in the CITY of 1837, whose six wards are drawn on printed page 46; it is not a location in the town of 1835 and does not place a house. What a match may carry, and it depends on WHICH TABLE it landed in. A match on printed page 38, or on any row of the mayors' table, is 1839-or-later evidence: it says the man held that office in that year and was therefore in Chicago in that year, it is written with the row's own describes_date and never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on it alone — a later appearance is corroboration of CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not of July 1835. A match on the sheriffs' rows of 1831, 1832, 1834 or 1836 is different in kind: the office is contemporary with the town, the 1834 row's term covers the scene date outright, and such a match carries reaches_scene. Even there the SOURCE is a retrospect — a table running to 1874, set in 1876 out of Old Settlers' recollections per the compiler's warning on printed page 3 — so it may be cited as a contemporary office and may not be graded `documented` without a second, nearer record. The ward on printed page 38 is a ward of the CITY of 1839 and places no house in the town of 1835. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Elston' folds to the same string as the 1837 entry's, and the given name of both begins D. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 1 time, as “ELSTON DANIEL”, 1836-06-18: 1 federal land entry — NE sec 08 T39N R14E, 160.00 acres stated in all, for $200.00 (ls0047). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: ELSTON DANIEL matches Daniel Elston: the residents layer holds exactly one person of the surname and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

resident_research.evidence_for: The University of Illinois finding aid identifies Daniel Elston as an English merchant arriving in Chicago in 1833 who manufactured soap and candles and later operated a distillery and brewery.
resident_research.notes: Candidate facts remain unasserted until a source bridges the candidate to the historical record by more than name similarity.

research_note: THE ONLY CHEMICAL WORKS IN THE 1835 DATASET, and the household that best shows what a single advertisement can imply about a population. A soap and candle manufactory buying tallow implies slaughtering (this dataset models three packing and slaughter buildings) and buying house ashes implies wood fires in a lot of houses, which is the population K1 is trying to count.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry.

address_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 prints this address against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Elston, Daniel, patent press-brick maker, res North Branch [died September 13, 1855, aged 65]'. It is evidence about 1843, written here as 1843's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.

back_projection.note: NOT READ BACK, BECAUSE SOMETHING BETTER ALREADY STANDS. Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 prints an address against this name in 1843, and it is left where it is. An 1835 placement already stands: this household works at `elston_soap_candle_manufactory`, and clause 2 says an attested 1835 placement always beats a door printed 8 years later. The later address stays on the record as 1843's evidence and moves nothing.

residence_back_projection.note: REFUSED, AND THE REFUSAL IS THE RECORD. Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 prints where this man lived in 1843 and this pass will not carry it back to 1835. The North Branch is the river, not a platted street. A refusal is written here rather than dropped so that a later run can see the address was read and ruled on, not missed (docs/RESIDENCE-BACK-PROJECTION.md, clause R4).
